title: The four immeasurables, now
tomorrow: can you give away the good you've done?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four truths, the handful of leaves: the ache, its cause, its ending, the way. Four truths, one path. Today, four ways of the heart that the path grows, and a question from two young men who could not stop arguing.
screen: `FOUR TRUTHS, ONE PATH.` → `FOUR WAYS OF THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Some group chats run on one question: whose version is right? Two young brahmins in the suttas, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, had that argument. Each said his own teacher knew the straight road to union with Brahma, the god their tradition honored. They couldn't settle it, so they took it to the Buddha. Here's the strange part. Union with Brahma was not the goal the Buddha taught. He could have waved the question away. Instead he gave them a road to Brahma. Why would he do that?
screen: `WHOSE VERSION IS RIGHT?` → `TWO BRAHMINS, ONE ARGUMENT.` → `A ROAD TO BRAHMA?`

segments.voice: First, in the Tevijja Sutta, he asks them a question back: has any teacher of yours seen Brahma face to face? No, they admit. Then it's like building a staircase to a mansion no one has seen. So he starts with what their own tradition says Brahma is like: free of hatred, free of ill will, master of himself. And he describes a heart that matches. It fills one direction with kindness, then the second, the third, the fourth, then above, below, everywhere, with no edge. Then the same with compassion, then gladness for others' good, then equanimity, a steadiness that doesn't tip. He compares it to a strong conch blower, heard in every direction at once. That's the puzzle solved. He met them in their own words and moved the road inside: a heart like Brahma's is the way to Brahma. That's the sense of the name Buddhists still use for these four: the brahmaviharas, Brahma's dwelling places. Their other name is the four immeasurables: metta, karuna, mudita, upekkha. Immeasurable because the sutta leaves no one out of them. Some readers find the third the hardest. Kindness to someone hurting comes easier than gladness for someone winning, especially when they won the thing you wanted.
screen: `HAS ANYONE SEEN BRAHMA?` · `A HEART LIKE BRAHMA'S.` · `EVERY DIRECTION, NO EDGE.` · `BRAHMA'S DWELLING PLACES.` · then, large: `IMMEASURABLE.`

segments.voice: Find a photo with people in it and rest your eyes on one face. Give that face the four in turn: may you be well; may your pain ease; I'm glad for your good things; and whatever comes, may you stay steady. Then move to the next face, and the next, the way the sutta moves from one direction to the next.
The four immeasurables: kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, a heart sent in every direction. Also called the brahmaviharas.
Your line: immeasurable. Kindness with the edges taken off, gladness included, no one left out. Day ten of the summit.

howItsDone: Buddhists practice the four immeasurables by sending kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity outward, often direction by direction or person by person, in sitting practice and in daily life.

match.prompt: four ways of the heart — tap the pairs.

myth: the Buddha told the brahmins their question about Brahma was pointless
he answered it, in their own words: a heart like Brahma's is the way to Brahma.
equanimity means not caring what happens to people
it's the fourth immeasurable, steadiness, sent out alongside kindness, not instead of it.
the brahmaviharas are named after Brahma
Brahma's dwelling places: the Tevijja story shows why the name fits.

fork.setup: you send kindness easily to friends, but skip the neighbor whose dog barks all night. what does 'immeasurable' ask of you here?
options: let the kindness reach him too: the sutta leaves no direction out.
kindness is for people who've earned it; friends first, the neighbor never.
equanimity covers him: stop noticing him, and no kindness is needed.
fork.reveal: the sutta fills every direction, above, below, everywhere, with no edge. immeasurable means no one is left out.

original.note: Pali: appamanna, the immeasurables, without measure or limit.

chat.says: roommate loved the four-truths text. but Ava got into the art program. i got waitlisted. happy for her… mostly
options: that's mudita, gladness at her good. it's grown, not faked. 'mostly' is a fine start.
kindness is what counts; gladness at her win is a nice extra you can skip.
equanimity means you shouldn't feel anything about it, so just stop caring.
chat.meaning: Mudita, gladness for another's good, is one of the four immeasurables the Buddha taught. Like the others, it grows by practice, one direction at a time.

tie.story: The Buddha told two brahmins the road to Brahma was a heart of kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, leaving no one out.
tie.friend: Mai can practice gladness for Ava, the hard third one, without pretending the waitlist doesn't sting.
tie.you: whose good news is hardest for you to be glad about?

Vasettha.meaning: one of the two young brahmins in the Tevijja Sutta

Brahma.meaning: a high god honored in the brahmins' tradition

brahmaviharas.meaning: Brahma's dwelling places: the four immeasurables

mudita.meaning: gladness at someone else's good fortune

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 13 (Tevijja Sutta: Vasettha and Bharadvaja; the way to union with Brahma)
Digha Nikaya 13, the four immeasurables pervading the directions, with the simile of the conch blower

notes: DN 13 paraphrased: Vasettha and Bharadvaja dispute which brahmin teaching leads to union with Brahma; no brahmin teacher has seen Brahma (the staircase to an unseen mansion); Brahma is described as free of hatred and ill will, self-mastered; the monk who pervades the directions with the four immeasurables is in harmony with Brahma. The conch-blower simile appears in DN 13. Confirm.
'The Buddha names no creator' follows the framing used on day 1784; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with it.

The four wishes in the practice are a description of the four immeasurables, not a quoted or composed prayer. The outline practice ('twenty minutes of the four') is sized to the app's two-minute sit; longer practice can be offered in 'go deeper'.
'Some readers find the third the hardest' replaces a 'for many people' claim (claims rule).
Shape: puzzle (why give brahmins a road to Brahma?). Answers day 1786's tomorrow. Mai's storyline: Ava got into the art program Mai was waitlisted for; mudita, unfinished ('mostly').
Surprising fact: the Tevijja Sutta shows why the brahmaviharas carry Brahma's name: a heart like Brahma's is the way to Brahma.
